headline: Approved research into possible purchase of two Northwest Conservation Area parcels totaling 54 acres.
summary: Members also approved $500 for Southwest trail markers and signs, and accepted NRPC's offer to host trail maps and QR codes. A pool proposal at 11 Lojko Drive will wait for a site visit on November 18, and the L Pine Street dog park will return for a recommendation on December 1.
decisions: Approved minutes of October 6, 2026 as amended by Commissioner Sarno.
Decided a site visit is needed before acting on the pool proposal at 11 Lojko Drive.
Requested a formal native landscape plan for the dog park pergola.
Approved research for a possible acquisition of two parcels totaling 54 acres from SPNHF.
Approved $1,050 payment of NHACC membership dues from the commission budget.
Approved up to $500 for trail markers and signage on the Southwest Trails.
Accepted NRPC's offer to host trail map files and manage QR code links, by consensus.

NASHUA CONSERVATION COMMISSION 
November 4, 2026 
 
A.  Call to order 
 
A regular meeting of the Nashua Conservation Commission was called 
to order on Wednesday, November 4, 2026 at 7:00 PM, 229 Main 
Street, City Hall. 
 
B.  Roll call  
 
Members present:  Sherry Dutzy, Chair 
                         Dick Widhu, Vice Chair 
Carol Sarno 
 Gloria McCarthy  
                         Brandon Pierotti 
  
 Will Darby (Absent) 
                         Amanda Griffith (Absent) 
                         Dale Carruth (Absent)  
                          
 
Also, in Attendance: Matt Sullivan, Community Development                                              
                     Director.   
                     Levent Akinci, Sustainability Planner. 
     
C.  Approval of minutes

E. New Business: 
 
Christine Sheridan, 11 Lojko Drive. Proposal to install a 20’ x 
36’ inground, gunite swimming pool within the wetland buffer of 
a critical wetland, with permanent impact to 572 SF of the 
wetland buffer. Map B. Lot 2818. Zone R-18 B – Suburban 
Residence. Ward 9. 
Christine Sheridan, homeowner at 11 Lojko Dr, presented a proposal 
to construct a 20-foot by 36-foot in-ground gunite swimming pool 
within the designated critical wetland buffer. Current backyard 
condition is completely flat lawn enclosed by mature arborvitae 
plantings. A small ditch/stream is situated directly behind the 
arborvitaes, designated on municipal GIS mapping as a critical 
wetland connecting through the subdivision to a prime wetland.  
The stream flows through the neighborhood via culverts under 
roadways, crossing behind adjacent rear yards. Neighboring 
properties also feature swimming pools. The 40-foot critical 
wetland buffer extends almost to the home’s rear foundation, 
encompassing nearly the entire back lawn. The house was 
constructed in 1995, but there are no physical wetland boundary 
monuments or posts in the yard. The custom gunite pool is planned 
for the right side of the backyard, customized to navigate 
underground obstructions such as potential buried tree stumps. 
The pool is proposed roughly 20 feet from the property line and 
approximately 6 to 10 feet from the ditch low point, remaining 
behind the mature arborvitae screen. 
 
COMMUNITY DEVELOPMENT DIRECTOR MATT SULLIVAN: We see this 
configuration in several subdivisions of this vintage. In the 
Southwest quad. We see sort of backlot drainage ditches that were 
intended to convey drainage. Once subdivisions were done, I think 
they were always intended to be man-made drainage ditches. What I 
think happened is through mapping exercises or frankly, just 
changes in character of the area in the rear lot, these have 
become labeled as critical wetlands. I don’t want to undermine 
your consideration of the application, but I think it’s 
conceivable that that shouldn’t even be under your jurisdiction. 
I really don’t believe this is a traditional wetland. I think it 
was created as a low point to convey drainage when the subdivision 
was done. 
 
The commission determined a site visit was necessary before acting 
on the application. 
 
The site visit is scheduled for Wednesday, November 18th at 4:00pm.

November 4, 2026 
Page 3  
 
       
   
City of Nashua, L Pine Street. Proposal to develop a public dog 
park, including 8 parking spaces, with permanent impact to 12,975 
SF of the wetland buffer for a prime wetland. Map 77. Lot 5. Zone 
R-B – Urban Residence. Ward 4. 
 
Jim Petropoulos, PE with (Hayner Swanson/ IMAG Corporation), and 
Matt Sullivan, Community Development Director presented a proposal 
for NIMCO industrial site (brownfield property) owned by the City 
of Nashua that was issued an RFP by the City several years ago 
for mixed-use/housing redevelopment. Lansing Melbourne Group 
(LMG) was selected as preferred developer approximately a year 
ago. As part of the public benefit negation within the development 
agreement, the city required the developer to construct a public 
dog park at this gateway to Mines Falls Park. The parcel had 
previously undergone a feasibility study 5 years ago conducted by 
the city’s animal and dog committee. Zoning is split north-south: 
the western portion is zoned Residential and the eastern portion 
is zoned General Industrial. Bordered on the north by the Nashua 
River, to the west and south by Mines Falls Park and backwater 
(“the cove”) and to the east by the Mill Yard District (Eversource 
substation, demolished NIMCO and Bagshaw buildings). Major site 
constraints include:  
• A 200-foot-tall active radio tower with three large guy wire 
stanchions/anchors arranged in a triangular pattern. 
• An extensive underground coper ground grid spreading beneath 
and around the radio tower. 
• A small radio tower utility shed requiring relocation. 
• A major overhead electric power line emerging from the 
Eversource substation along the eastern boundary, governed 
by an Eversource easement  
 
The wetland delineation and buffer were flagged by Gove 
Environmental Services and flagged the top of the riverbank. The 
project is subject to the City’s 75-foot primary wetland/shoreline 
buffer. The existing buffer condition is heavily distributed and 
altered, consisting of an existing paved path ending on the east, 
transitioning into a gravel access roadway entering Mines Falls 
Park. Most of the subjected parcel is located inside the 100-year 
floodplain and the floodway of the Nashua River (historical 
flooding observed in the back-to-back storms of 2006 and 2007, 
and in 1985. The dog park encompasses approximately 1.0 acres, 
entirely fenced in. Segregated zones for small dogs and large dogs 
in the northern half, surfaced with pea stone ground cover. The 
southern half will be maintained as lawn cover. An engineered
NCC 
November 4, 2026 
Page 4  
 
drainage swale feature bisects the park interior to manage surface 
flows and add varied terrain. An open-air curved pergola structure 
at the entrance will provide shaded seating, hardscaping, 
informational signage, and landscaping plantings. Access provided 
from the extension of Spine Road (to be accepted as a public 
street) down a steep 10% grade slope into 8 paved parking spaces. 
Existing paved surface within the wetland buffer is 4,625 sq. ft 
Proposed project will result in 8,125 sq. ft of impervious surface 
(an increase of approximately 3,500 to 3,600 sq. ft, nearly 
doubling impervious cover). Total buffer impact area is 12,000 to 
13,000 sq. ft No direct fill or dredge impacts within the Nashua 
River or delineated wetlands. The stormwater drainage currently 
runs off untreated directly into the river. The plan introduces a 
catch basin at the low point of the paved parking lot routed 
through a mechanical qualitative treatment device (filtering 
suspended solids, oils, and sediment). The treatment discharge 
connects to an existing 54-inch stormwater culvert and large 
concrete headwall. Rather than constructing a new headwall breach 
along the bank, the project will core a 15-inch opening into the 
existing concrete wingwall. A hydrologist has been retained to 
preform zero-rise hydraulic calculations to verify that proposed 
grading within the floodway will not elevate the base flood 
elevations.   
 
DISCUSSION INSUED ON SHIFTING THE PARKING LOT TO THE WEST SIDE OF 
THE LOT, THREE SPECIES OF TURTLES FOUND IN THE AREA, AND PARKING-
LOT SURFACING. 
 
Commissioner Dutzy questioned why the parking area could not 
remain packed gravel or permeable pavement to minimize impervious 
footprint. 
 
Matt Sullivan noted DPW preference for asphalt for long-term 25-
year durability and ease of snow maintenance, stating the pervious 
pavement carries severe maintenance burdens and high failure rates 
in municipal settings. Loose stone would be plowed into 
surrounding lawn during winter. The dog park will most likely be 
maintained and plowed year-round, serving as winter access for 
snowshoer’s entering Mine Falls Park. 
 
DISCUSSION INSUED ON DE-ICING ALTERNATIVES TO PREVENT DOG PAW 
INJURIES AND RIVER POLLUTION, MAKING JUST THE PARKING SPACES 
GRAVEL AND ASPESTOS TESTING IN THE DOG PARK.  
 
Commissioner Dutzy noted extensive Japanese knotweed colonies 
along the southwest portion near the Eversource easement and up 
Spine Road.
NCC 
November 4, 2026 
Page 5  
 
 
Matt Sullivan stated the expanded Riverfront Tax Increment Finance 
(TIF)District funds ongoing invasive species eradication along 
the riverfront, which can be applied to maintain the area. The 
developer has agreed to include buffer cleanup (removing urban 
debris/trash), removing riverbank invasive’s, and installing 
permanent Conservation Commission boundary markers along the tree 
line.    
 
The Commission requested a formal landscape plan consisting 
exclusively of native pollinator shrubs, flowering species, and 
winter food sources for birds around the pergola.  
 
Site walk was scheduled for Monday November 23rd at 4:00pm. 
Participants are asked to park at the base of Spine Road. Applicant 
will return to the Conservation Commission agenda on December 1st 
2026 for formal recommendation to the Zoning Board of Adjustments.  
 
DISCUSSION INSUED ABOUT THE DOG PARK BEING 100% PUBLIC, NOT 
PRIVATE OR RESTRICTED TO APAPRTMENT TENANTS. AND POSSIBLITY OF A 
NONPROFIT FORM TO SUPPORT THE PARK.  
 
 
F. NCC Correspondence and Communications 
 
CITY OF NASHUA, 1 PINE STREET EXTENSION (NIMCO)-INFORMATIONAL ONLY 
NO VOTE: 
 
Jim Petropoulos presented an informational presentation regarding 
the redevelopment of the former NIMCO industrial footprint 
directly north of the dog park. Project involves the construction 
of (2) multi-story residential buildings totaling approximately 
250 units, ranging in height from (5-7) stories. Building (1) 
closest to the Nashua River, will feature (4-5) stories of 
residential living constructed over structured parking, topped 
with an outdoor elevated promenade overlooking the river corridor 
to the west (similar to the High Street development). Building 2 
will feature a mix of under-structure parking and surface parking. 
Temporary parking at the southern edge will support construction 
and phased staging, ultimately planned in phase 2 to become 
central community park. The parcel falls under the Urban Shoreland 
Protection exemption, requiring no local buffer voting action by 
the Commission. The 75-foot primary river setback line sits 
immediately adjacent to the building footprint. The area within 
the 75-foot buffer consists of an existing paved access drive (to 
be maintained for emergency life safety access) and an overhead 
Eversource transmission line corridor. Pedestrian connectivity is
NCC 
November 4, 2026 
Page 6  
 
designated to transition north into a path linking the Millyard 
Technology Park and integrating into the municipal Riverwalk 
network.  
 
Commissioners strongly advocated for including private 
residential balconies on the river-facing facades, noting recent 
developments in Nashua lack access to outdoor air.  
 
Jim Petropoulos confirmed building (2) includes balconies and will 
verify plans for building (1), while noting significant shared 
outdoor deck/grilling amenities are incorporated. 
  
SPNHF DISCUSSION; LAND ACUISITION (NORTHWEST PROPERTIES): 
 
Carrie Deegan, Stewardship and Recreation Department, Society for 
the Protection of New Hampshire Forests (SPNHF) and Stacy 
Hernandez, Land Conservation Manager, SPNHF, presented the SPNHF 
proposed transferring fee ownership of (2) parcels (totaling 54 
acres) within the Northwest Conservation Area to the City of 
Nashua/Conservation Commission: 
 
• Parcel (1) H635: 41 acres abutting existing City of Nashua 
conservation land, featuring and existing conservation 
easement held by the City of Nashua with an executory 
interest held by the Land and Community Heritage Investment 
Program (LCHIP) 
• Parcel (2) 13 acres abutting the YMCA and Westwood Park 
industrial area, encumbered by a 1998 deed restriction. 
 
Acquired by SPNHF in December 2015 as a donation from Westwood 
Park LLC (Stabile/Stanley). The forest Society accepted fee title 
with the express intent to transfer ownership to Pennichuck Water 
Works or the City of Nashua once permanently projected. The 
transfer stalled in 2015-2016 because the City was actively 
negotiating the municipal acquisition of Pennichuck Corporation. 
The parcels are small and isolated compared to SPNHF’s typical 
statewide working forest reservations (over 120 properties 
statewide), making municipal ownership by an abutting conservation 
holder far more practical. They are considered high-value 
conservation land: Designated at Tier 1 Habitat (highest quality 
habitat in the state) under the New Hampshire Fish & Game Wildlife 
Action Plan. Situated directly over a major stratified drift 
aquifer critical for reginal drinking water supply and quality 
protection for Pennichuck Brook tributaries. Appraised market 
value in 2015 was established at $150,000 even with preexisting 
deed restrictions and easements. The 41-acre parcel is already
NCC 
November 4, 2026 
Page 7  
 
actively monitored by the Nashua Conservation Commission for 
annual LCHIP reporting. The 13-acre parcel experienced an 
unauthorized homeless encampment, and installed a chain gate and 
log barriers to block vehicle access. The site is currently clean 
and secure. SPNHF spent considerable funds on due diligence during 
the 2015 acquisition, including boundary surveys, title work, and 
phase 1 Environmental Hazardous Waste Assessments conforming to 
Land Trust Alliance standards. While SPNHF would appreciate 
reimbursement of administrative/ due diligence costs from the 
Conservation Commission funds, they explicitly clarified that 
financial reimbursement is not a deal breaker for the transfer.    
 
A motion was made by Commissioner Dutzy to move for the 
Conservation Commission to proceed with research needed for a 
possible acquisition of these (2) parcels of land. 
 
Seconded by, Commissioner Widue. 
 
MOTION CARRIES 
 
DISCUSION INSUED ABOUT NEXT STEPS FOR LEVENT AKINCI TO COORDINATE 
WITH SPNHF STAFF AND CITY LEGAL TO PREP TRANSFER DOCUMENTS. 
 
 
CITY TAX AUCTION PARCEL I-10 TRANSFER: 
 
Levent Akinci reported that Parcel I-10 was retained by the City 
following an unpaid tax auction where no private bids were 
submitted. The parcel is a landlocked interior sliver surrounded 
by municipal conservation land, having no viable independent use 
or development capability. Custody and control of parcel I-10 will 
formally transfer to the Conservation Commission to consolidate 
contiguous protected open space. No specialized easement 
monitoring is required.  
 
NASHUA RE-CODE: CIVIC SPACE vs. CONSERVATION OPEN SPACE 
DESIGNATION:  
 
Levent Akinci presented an informational briefing regarding draft 
zoning maps under the city-wide Re-Code project, clarifying 
distinctions between (2) public land classifications: 
 
• Civic Space: Dedicated park facilities containing active 
amenities, play equipment, sports fields, or public 
infrastructure; maintained under jurisdiction of the 
Department of Public Works (DPW)/ Parks and Recreation.
NCC 
November 4, 2026 
Page 8  
 
• Conservation Open Space: Protected natural conservation 
lands, forests, and wetlands managed under the regulatory 
authority of the Conservation Commission. 
 
Map Corrections identified by commissioners: 
• Maplewood subdivision open space 
• Buckmeadow 
• Cherrywood 
• Yudicky Park  
 
G. Commissioners Discussion 
NHACC MEMEBRSHIP DUES RENEWAL: 
 
Commissioner Dutzy spoke about the annual membership invoice 
received from the New Hampshire Association of Conservation 
Commissions (NHACC) for $1,050. 
Motion made by Commissioner Dutzy to approve payment of the NHACC 
invoice in the amount of $1,050 from the commission budget. 
 
Seconded by Commissioner Sarno 
 
MOTION CARRIES 
 
SOUTHWEST TRAILS EXPENSE AUTHORIZATION FOR TRAILBLAZING AND 
SIGNAGE: 
 
Funding request was made by Commissioner Widhue to reimburse trail 
marking expenses and purchase new interpretive trail signage 
across the Southwest Conservation trails network: 
• Prior trail blazing markers incurred $241 unreimbursed 
expenses.  
• Additional funds required for newly designed signs and 
mounting hardware, pending completion of updated QR codes. 
 
Motion to approve made by Commissioner Dutzy, budget not to exceed 
$500 for trailblazing and signage for the Southwest Trails. 
 
Seconded by Commissioner Sarno 
 
MOTION CARRIES

Commissioner Dutzy and Commissioner Widhu spoke about the

monitoring of city-held conservation easements scheduled for 
November 21st, starting at 10:00am. Commissioner noted the walk 
falls during active firearm deer hunting season (ending December 
1st); all participants must wear high-visibility blaze orange vest

• Inspection team assignments:  
Team 1 (Massasoit Parcels): Commissioner Darby, Brandan and

Team 2 (Northwest Conservation Parcels H635, Farley Road,

entrance conditions and inspect the posted 13 acres 
YMCA/Westwood buffer area.  
 
VOLUNTEER WORKDAY AND INVASIVE SPECIES REMOVAL AT TERRELL 
HOMESTEAD:  
 
Commissioner Sarno discussed that this will be held on Wednesday 
November 5th 9:30am-12:15pm. Operational focus: hand-pulling 
oriental bittersweet vines, with dedicated student teams stripping 
and bagging mature fruiting berries to prevent seed propagation 
in the meadow. 
 
BUCKMEADOW BRUSH HOGGING OPERATIONS AND FIELD RUTTING INCIDENT: 
 
Commissioner Sarno discussed that the new vender hired to brush 
hog Buckmeadow had some of their heavy equipment get stuck. The 
contractor attempted to winch the equipment using their own 
service trucks, which also became stuck, requiring heavy 
commercial tow trucks to extract the machinery. The extraction 
left visible ruts and soil displacement in the meadow. A trail 
user filed a complaint with Community Development, which staff 
addressed.   
Commissioner Sarno conducted a field inspection and took some 
video of the area. The contractor offered to return with hand 
rakes to grade out and smooth the ruts. Commissioner Sarno noted 
that while the ruts are unsightly, the native wet meadow 
vegetation will likely naturally regenerate and heal during the 
spring growing season without mechanical intervention that could 
cause further compaction. Commissioner Sarno with upload the video 
to the municipal server for commissioners to inspect before 
determining whether to accept the contractors offer to rake.

NRPC WEBSITE HOSTING FOR TRAIL MAPS AND QR CODES: 
 
Commissioner Sarno spoke about a technical issue with squarespace 
that creates the QR codes for trail maps and brochures. NRPC 
offered to permanently host the official trail brochures and maps 
on NRPC server at zero charge to the city.  
 
The commission unanimously agreed by consensus to accept NRPC’s 
offer to host the digital trail map files and manage the QR code 
links.
